title: Category 3 Deep-learning vision models and applications
text:
A vision foundation model is a large image encoder pretrained on broad image collections so that its internal features can be reused for many later tasks. Vision Transformers divide an image into patches, treat those patches as tokens and learn relationships among them. Self-supervised models such as DINO learn useful visual structure without requiring a class label for every pretraining image.
In these projects, students do not train a foundation model from the beginning. They use a pretrained backbone as a frozen feature extractor and train only a small prediction head or adapter. For land-cover classification, the representation may separate forests, rivers and residential areas. For industrial inspection, patch-level representations may show where a surface differs from normal examples.
The central evaluation separates what the pretrained backbone already provides from what the student’s adaptation contributes. A frozen linear probe, a lightweight adapter and—where feasible—a full fine-tune are compared using the same labels, split and backbone. Performance is reported together with the number of trainable parameters and compute cost.

title: Category 3 Deep-learning vision models and applications
text:
Learn first and find ideas

Core reading: DINO, DINOv2, the DINOv2 model card and code, DINOv3 and AnomalyDINO.
Data and model hubs: MVTec AD, EuroSAT, Hugging Face models and timm.
Keep zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot and full-shot anomaly results separate, and never compare an image-level metric directly with a pixel-level metric.

title: Category 3 Deep-learning vision models and applications
section: 3.1 Adapting DINO backbones for land cover or industrial anomalies
text:
3.1 Adapting DINO backbones for land cover or industrial anomalies

TaskImage classification or image/pixel anomaly detection Recommended levelBSc or MSc with separate tracks ComputeModerate; frozen ViT-S practical on 8 GB, dense MSc work may need more Starting paperOquab et al., DINOv2, 2023


What you will do. Use a pretrained self-supervised vision transformer as a frozen feature extractor. Train a small head or adapter for a specialised task. Measure the performance of frozen features and test whether an adapter still contributes when a newer backbone is used.

Project goal. Quantify the trade-off among task performance, number of trainable parameters and supervision. Choose one track: EuroSAT RGB land-cover classification or MVTec industrial anomaly detection/localisation.
Data. BSc/default classification track: EuroSAT, 27,000 Sentinel-2 patches in 10 classes. Use the RGB version for ordinary DINO backbones; the 13-band version requires an explicit multispectral adapter and is a separate MSc question. MSc anomaly track: MVTec AD, more than 5,000 images in 15 categories with pixel masks, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for non-commercial research.
Methods and starting code. Default to DINOv2 ViT-S/14 from the official Apache-2.0 repository and model card. Compare frozen linear/MLP probes, k-NN or AnomalyDINO patch similarity, and a lightweight multi-scale adapter. DINOv3 is optional through the official repository; its weights are gated under a custom Meta licence.
Required baselines. From-scratch CNN, ImageNet-pretrained ResNet or ViT, frozen DINOv2 with no adapter, lightweight adapter and full fine-tuning only if hardware permits. On MVTec, include a simple nearest-neighbour patch baseline and keep zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot and full-shot protocols separate.
Evaluation. EuroSAT: top-1 accuracy, macro-F1, label-efficiency curve and trainable parameters. MVTec: image AUROC plus pixel AUROC/PRO or pixel F1-max, reported by category and protocol. Measure inference memory/latency. Never compare a one-shot image metric directly with a zero-shot pixel metric.

Bachelor scope. Use EuroSAT RGB. Compare a frozen DINOv2 ViT-S linear probe with an ImageNet-pretrained CNN and, if feasible, a small adapter at several label budgets.


Master research question and contribution. Choose one question. Dense anomaly route: can a supervised multi-scale adapter over frozen patch tokens improve few-shot localisation at a fixed label and parameter budget, and does the gain remain after switching DINOv2 to DINOv3? Remote-sensing route: can a small multispectral input adapter exploit 13 bands without full backbone fine-tuning? Report cross-version or cross-band ablations so the adapter’s value is isolated.

Practical notes. Do not attempt DINOv3 ViT-7B. DINOv2 is ungated and Apache 2.0; build the pipeline on it first. DINOv3’s licence is non-standard and gated but not stated as categorically non-commercial; an industry use requires institutional/legal review. MVTec itself is non-commercial, so it cannot serve as an industry dataset without separate permission.

title: Category 2 Self-supervised representation learning for time series
text:
A time series is an ordered sequence of measurements. A wearable device may record acceleration every fraction of a second, an ECG contains voltage measurements from several leads, and an industrial plant records pressure, flow, temperature and energy over time. These signals contain repeated patterns, trends and operating phases, but useful labels—such as a person’s activity, a diagnosis or an abnormal production cycle—may require expert work and are often scarce.
Self-supervised learning (SSL) learns from the unlabelled recordings by creating its own training task. A model might make two valid views of the same signal agree, hide part of a sequence and predict it, or predict the representation of a future segment. The resulting encoder converts a variable-length recording or window into a compact numerical representation. A small classification or regression head is then trained for a downstream task—for example, recognising an activity or predicting a filtration cycle’s final energy use.
The important question is not whether the pretraining loss decreases, but whether the learned representation reduces the amount of labelled data needed and transfers to new people, machines or operating conditions. Every project therefore compares SSL with a fully supervised model and a randomly initialised encoder on leakage-safe splits.

title: Category 2 Self-supervised representation learning for time series
text:
Learn first and find ideas

Methods with code: TS-TCC, TS2Vec, TF-C and SimMTM.
Data sources: UCI Machine Learning Repository, PhysioNet, UCR/UEA archive, Monash forecasting archive and Zenodo.
Monitor embedding variance and covariance from the first epoch in latent-predictive work. A smooth pretraining loss does not establish that the representation is useful.

title: Category 2 Self-supervised representation learning for time series
section: 2.1 Tetra Pak industrial collaboration: Regime-aware self-supervised learning for non-stationary filtration cycles
text:
2.1 Tetra Pak industrial collaboration: Regime-aware self-supervised learning for non-stationary filtration cycles

Project settingIndustrial collaboration with Tetra Pak; partner-supplied data under an approved agreement TaskSelf-supervised multivariate time-series learning followed by cycle-level regression or anomaly detection Recommended levelBSc or MSc; scope confirmed after an initial data profile ComputeLight to moderate; compact models on a 4-8 GB GPU Starting paperYue et al., TS2Vec, AAAI 2022


What you will do. Membrane-filtration plants generate repeated production and cleaning cycles containing flow, pressure, temperature and energy measurements. Earlier work found substantial cycle-to-cycle differences. The student will identify whether these reflect operating settings, process phases, fouling, sensor drift or abnormal operation, then learn representations that account for the resulting regimes.

Project goal. Test whether regime-aware self-supervised pretraining improves low-label prediction and transfer. The preferred task is early prediction of final specific energy consumption, such as electrical energy per unit of permeate or product. If that target cannot be constructed, use regime-conditioned anomaly detection.
Data. Tetra Pak will provide anonymised process data or an approved secure environment; the data are not public. Sources may include customer production for one product, pilot-plant trials or a new installation. Requested signals include flow, pressure, temperature, power or energy, setpoints, product/line/phase identifiers, cycle boundaries and available alarms or cleaning records. The current estimate is a few months of approximately minute-level data; the exact installation, channels and usable-cycle count must be confirmed.
Methods and starting code. Start with TS2Vec and code, TS-TCC and code, or SimMTM and code, using a compact 1-D CNN, TCN or GRU. The MSc method should make positive pairs or masks aware of cycle phase and regime, or condition the encoder on product, line and setpoints. Use change-point detection, clustering and PCA/UMAP for the initial regime analysis.
Required baselines. Regime-specific mean or running energy extrapolation; XGBoost or linear regression on cycle-prefix features; supervised TCN/GRU; generic SSL across all cycles; and a per-regime or regime-conditioned model. Include random-frozen, frozen-probe, fine-tuned and fully supervised controls when labels support them.
Evaluation. Split by complete cycle and preserve time order; never place windows from one cycle in both training and test sets. For energy regression, report MAE, RMSE and normalized MAE when predicting final specific energy from fixed prefixes such as 20%, 30% and 50%. Test a held-out period, line, product or regime where possible. For anomalies, use AUPRC plus precision and recall at an agreed alert budget. Include label-efficiency budgets and at least three seeds where sample size permits.

Bachelor scope. Profile and segment cycles, identify operating regimes, implement one supervised baseline and one established SSL method, and evaluate one target. Compare a global model with a regime-specific or conditioned variant and include one process-aware view or masking ablation. No new architecture is required.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Can cycle-phase and operating-regime-aware self-supervised views separate legitimate cycle variation from energy inefficiency or abnormal behaviour better than generic augmentations? Compare global, per-regime and conditioned encoders at matched capacity; define positives or masks using process context; and test label efficiency plus held-out-regime transfer. The contribution is the regime-aware representation and analysis, not an unchanged TS2Vec or TS-TCC run.

Practical notes. First confirm cycle boundaries, units, synchronization, missingness, regime metadata, independent-cycle count and one defensible target. Overlapping windows do not replace independent cycles. Avoid trivial full-cycle energy calculation by forecasting early or using normalized efficiency. Data and trained artefacts remain subject to the AU-Tetra Pak agreement.

title: Category 2 Self-supervised representation learning for time series
section: 2.2 Contrastive learning for wearable activity recognition
text:
2.2 Contrastive learning for wearable activity recognition

TaskSelf-supervised time-series representation learning then classification Recommended levelBSc or MSc ComputeLight; CPU or 4 GB GPU Starting paperEldele et al., TS-TCC, IJCAI 2021


What you will do. A phone records multi-channel acceleration and angular velocity while a person walks, sits or climbs stairs. Learn an encoder from the unlabelled sensor windows, freeze it and ask whether a small classifier can recognise activities with few labels.

Project goal. Test whether self-supervised representations approach a fully supervised classifier at 1%, 5%, 10% and 100% label budgets and whether physically plausible sensor views improve orientation robustness.
Data. Use UCI Human Activity Recognition: 30 subjects, six activities, 10,299 windows, 50 Hz inertial data and a subject-independent standard split. The download is about 58 MB and is CC BY 4.0.
Methods and starting code. TS-TCC with the official code, TS2Vec with official code, and optionally CA-TCC. Use the same 1-D CNN or small Transformer encoder in SSL and supervised comparisons.
Required baselines. Random frozen encoder, SSL frozen linear probe, SSL fine-tuning and fully supervised end-to-end training. A simple feature-based classifier is a useful sanity check.
Evaluation. Accuracy and macro-F1 on subject-independent splits, label-efficiency curves and at least three seeds. For robustness, jointly rotate accelerometer and gyroscope triads at test time and measure degradation.

Bachelor scope. Reproduce TS-TCC or TS2Vec, compare frozen and fine-tuned representations with supervised training and produce the full label-efficiency curve.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Do physics-consistent SO(3) orientation views improve label efficiency and robustness more than signal-agnostic jitter, scaling and permutation? Separate gravity from body acceleration, rotate coupled sensor triads consistently, and ablate each step. The insight comes from physically valid view construction, not tuning augmentation strength.

Practical notes. The dataset is small and includes a standard subject-independent split. Preserve subject grouping; never split windows from the same subject across train and test.

title: Category 2 Self-supervised representation learning for time series
text:
2.3 Lead-aware masked learning for 12-lead ECG

TaskSelf-supervised multivariate time-series learning then multi-label classification Recommended levelMSc preferred; BSc comparator variant ComputeModerate; 8 GB GPU recommended Starting paperDong et al., SimMTM, NeurIPS 2023


What you will do. A 12-lead ECG observes the same cardiac event from different electrical viewpoints. Instead of masking arbitrary time patches, the model hides complete leads or anatomical lead groups and predicts their latent representations from the visible leads.

Project goal. Compare contrastive and masked/latent-predictive pretraining under low-label conditions and determine whether lead-aware masking learns cross-lead physiology rather than local interpolation.
Data. Use PTB-XL: 21,799 ten-second ECGs from 18,869 patients, available at 100 and 500 Hz under CC BY 4.0 without credentialing. Use folds 1–8 for training, 9 for validation and 10 for testing; these are patient-aware.
Methods and starting code. Begin with SimMTM official code, TF-C with official code, or TS2Vec. A 1-D ResNet or compact Transformer is the shared encoder. JEPA-style work is an MSc extension and must be described as based on recent preprints rather than an established benchmark.
Required baselines. Random frozen encoder, frozen probe, fine-tuning and the same encoder fully supervised. Compare random temporal masking with complete-lead and anatomical-group masking.
Evaluation. Macro-AUROC on fold 10 for the five diagnostic superclasses is the recommended primary endpoint; add macro-AUPRC for imbalance. Report 1/10/100% label budgets, multiple seeds and patient-level splits. Monitor embedding variance and covariance during latent-predictive training.

Bachelor scope. Reproduce one stable masked method such as SimMTM against TS2Vec and supervised training on the five superclasses. JEPA is not required.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Can a lead-identity-conditioned predictor reconstruct the latent representation of missing leads without collapse, and does that improve low-label diagnosis? Develop lead/group masking, predictor conditioning and collapse diagnostics; ablate masking granularity, EMA schedule and predictor depth. Cross-dataset transfer is optional only after the core study works.

Practical notes. This is methodologically risky because structured masking can collapse. Start at 100 Hz and five superclasses. Keep patient grouping and class definitions identical across methods.

title: Category 2 Self-supervised representation learning for time series
section: 2.4 Self-supervised forecasting representations for energy series
text:
2.4 Self-supervised forecasting representations for energy series

TaskSelf-supervised time-series learning then temporal regression Recommended levelBSc or MSc ComputeLight to moderate; 4–8 GB GPU Starting paperWoo et al., CoST, ICLR 2022


What you will do. Pretrain an encoder on unlabelled energy or transformer measurements, freeze it and fit a small forecasting head. The core comparison asks whether a reusable representation competes with a purpose-built supervised forecaster when labels or trainable parameters are restricted.

Project goal. Evaluate representation quality across several forecast horizons and determine whether season/trend-aware positive pairs help under low-label or transfer settings.
Data. Primary benchmark: ETT from the official ETDataset repository, using ETTh1/ETTh2 or ETTm1/ETTm2 with chronological splits. Optional external-validity set: UCI household power consumption, about 2.1 million minute readings from one household. It supports chronological forecasting, not household-level classification or cross-household claims.
Methods and starting code. CoST, TS2Vec and SimMTM. Use DLinear and PatchTST as supervised reference models. A ridge or linear head on frozen representations is the key diagnostic.
Required baselines. Seasonal-naive forecast, DLinear, PatchTST, random frozen encoder, frozen SSL head and SSL fine-tuning. Use identical input lengths and chronological splits.
Evaluation. MSE and MAE at agreed horizons such as 24/48/168/336/720 where the dataset supports them. Report label/data-efficiency curves, three seeds and training cost. Beating PatchTST is not a project requirement; analyse why the methods differ.

Bachelor scope. Reproduce CoST or TS2Vec on one ETT subset and compare a frozen linear head with DLinear/PatchTST. Add one second horizon or dataset only after the pipeline is stable.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Do decomposition-aligned positive pairs improve transfer and low-data forecasting when seasonal phase drifts? Use a stable period or seasonal decomposition to select positives, compare it with random cropping and frequency-domain contrast, and analyse failure on non-stationary intervals. A negative result is useful if it reveals when estimated seasonality is unreliable.

Practical notes. Period estimation can become the whole thesis. Validate on clean ETT seasonality before using irregular household behaviour. Fit decomposition and normalization on training time only.

Back to category introduction ↑

title: Category 2 Self-supervised representation learning for time series
section: 2.5 Self-supervised learning on heat-pump smart-meter data
text:
2.5 Self-supervised learning on heat-pump smart-meter data

TaskTime-series representation learning then household-level classification Recommended levelBSc or MSc, subject to a licence and data check ComputeLight to moderate after preprocessing Starting paperBrudermueller et al., HEAPO dataset paper, 2025


What you will do. Pretrain on a large pool of unlabelled household electricity streams, then use a small labelled subset to classify heat-pump type or operational faults. Candidate extensions can define views that account for weather and thermostatic cycling.

Project goal. Determine whether pretraining on unlabelled control households improves label efficiency on the 214 treatment households with smart-meter data and inspection information.
Data. Use HEAPO on Zenodo, with 1,408 households, and the official MIT-licensed code/dataloader. The paper reports 214 treatment and 1,194 control households plus 410 inspection protocols. The Zenodo Rights metadata does not display a dataset licence as of 16 September 2026; the paper’s CC BY 4.0 licence does not automatically license the data. Confirm reuse terms with the depositor before starting the project.
Methods and starting code. TS2Vec, TS-TCC and SimMTM or another masked model, optionally weather-conditioned. Use a 1-D CNN, InceptionTime or LSTM as the supervised model. Start with heat-pump type or a sufficiently prevalent protocol label.
Required baselines. Random frozen encoder, frozen SSL probe, SSL fine-tuning and end-to-end supervised training on identical grouped splits. Weather-only and metadata-only baselines help determine what the load series adds.
Evaluation. Group by household. Use balanced accuracy and macro-F1 for heat-pump type; macro-F1 and per-label AUROC/AUPRC for faults. Plot 1/5/10/100% label budgets. Disaggregation is a stretch only after counting households with a dedicated heat-pump meter; use nMAE/nRMSE if the subset is adequate.

Bachelor scope. After the licence check, choose one classification task, one SSL encoder and one supervised baseline. The deliverable is grouped evaluation and a label-efficiency curve.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Do outdoor-temperature-matched positives and whole-cycle masking learn heat-pump behaviour more effectively than generic jitter and random masking? Implement one or both physics-aware views, ablate weather conditioning and compare across household groups. Disaggregation should not be the core question unless the submetered cohort is large enough.

Practical notes. Before starting, verify the dataset licence, field definitions, label prevalence, missingness and the number of households with a dedicated heat-pump meter. If reuse terms cannot be clarified, select another dataset.

Back to category introduction ↑

title: Category 2 Self-supervised representation learning for time series
section: 2.6 Graph self-supervised learning from vibration signals
text:
2.6 Graph self-supervised learning from vibration signals

TaskGraph-level classification with cross-condition transfer Recommended levelMSc preferred; BSc supervised variant ComputeModerate preprocessing; small models on 4–8 GB GPU Starting paperHou et al., GraphMAE, KDD 2022


What you will do. Convert bearing vibration windows into graphs, pretrain a graph encoder without fault labels and test whether the representation transfers across load or speed conditions better than a raw-signal CNN.

Project goal. Separate two effects: whether the graph construction is useful and whether self-supervision adds value once that graph is fixed.
Data. Reproduction set: CWRU Bearing Data Center. MSc set: Paderborn KAt with 32 bearings, four operating conditions and 64 kHz vibration plus speed/torque/load channels; downloads. Paderborn is about 5 GB and is documented as CC BY-NC 4.0 for non-commercial academic use in the source publication.
Methods and starting code. GraphMAE or BGRL on window graphs, a supervised GNN on the same graphs and a 1-D CNN on raw vibration. Use order tracking, envelope spectra and coherence for the MSc physics graph.
Required baselines. Raw-signal 1-D CNN, supervised GNN on the exact same graph, random frozen graph encoder and SSL frozen/fine-tuned encoders. Compare physics-grounded edges with naive similarity and random edges.
Evaluation. Accuracy and macro-F1. Report in-distribution performance, but make cross-operating-condition transfer decisive: train on one condition and test on another using bearing-level grouping and identical held-out conditions for every method.

Bachelor scope. Use CWRU to build a supervised GNN fault classifier with a simple similarity graph, compare it with a 1-D CNN and randomize the edges once.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Does a graph built from order-tracked fault-frequency sub-bands and spectral coherence transfer better across operating conditions than an ad hoc similarity graph? Compute BPFO/BPFI/BSF from bearing geometry and shaft speed, define a defensible thresholding rule, then evaluate supervised and SSL encoders. The signal-processing graph is the contribution; GraphMAE is a baseline.

Practical notes. This project requires substantial signal preprocessing. Confirm the 5 GB Paderborn download before work begins. Split by bearing, not by windows; otherwise neighbouring samples from the same physical bearing will leak across sets.

title: BSc and MSc Student Project Portfolio
text:
Shared protocol for self-supervised projects
Every self-supervised or pretrained project should report these settings whenever they are meaningful:

Frozen linear evaluation. Pretrain without labels, freeze the encoder and train only a lightweight head.
Fine-tuning. Initialise from the pretrained encoder and update it with labels.
Fully supervised baseline. Train the same encoder architecture from scratch using labels.
Random-initialisation control. Freeze a randomly initialised encoder and train the same head.
Label-efficiency curve. Report several label budgets, typically 1%, 5%, 10% and 100%.


Leakage rule. Group splits by the real independent unit: subject, patient, household, engine, bearing or process cycle—never by window. On graphs, state whether pretraining is transductive or strict inductive. On forecasting tasks, preserve chronological order.

title: Category 4 Signal processing and deep-unfolded models
text:
Many classical signal-processing methods are iterative optimisation algorithms: a decomposition, reconstruction or filtering result is obtained by repeating a fixed update rule until convergence, using hyperparameters that are set once and applied to every signal. Algorithm unrolling, also called deep unfolding, rewrites a fixed number of iterations of such an algorithm as the layers of a neural network. The algorithm’s update equations fix the network’s architecture, so the model stays interpretable, while its hyperparameters become trainable weights, learned end to end from data instead of tuned once by hand.
This differs from the representation-learning projects in Category 2: there, a generic encoder learns a representation through a self-supervised pretext task. Here, the network architecture itself is a classical algorithm, truncated to a handful of layers and made learnable. The typical finding across the field is that a handful of unrolled, learned iterations matches or beats an algorithm run to full convergence with a fixed hyperparameter, at a fraction of the compute.

title: Category 4 Signal processing and deep-unfolded models
text:
Learn first and find ideas

General unrolling: Gregor & LeCun, Learning Fast Approximations of Sparse Coding (LISTA), ICML 2010 — the founding example, unrolling ISTA. Monga, Li & Eldar, Algorithm Unrolling: Interpretable, Efficient Deep Learning for Signal and Image Processing, IEEE SPM 2021 — the field’s main survey. Yang, Sun, Li & Xu, Deep ADMM-Net for Compressive Sensing MRI, NeurIPS 2016 — unrolling a coupled, multi-variable ADMM iteration.
Signal decomposition: Dragomiretskiy & Zosso, Variational Mode Decomposition, IEEE TSP 2014, and reference Python code. Rehman & Aftab, Multivariate Variational Mode Decomposition, IEEE TSP 2019.
Ahmad, Wesemann, Waschkowski & Khalid, Robust Spatiotemporal Forecasting Using Adaptive Deep-Unfolded VMD, 2025, and official code — the anchor paper for Project 4.1, unrolling single-channel VMD.

title: Category 4 Signal processing and deep-unfolded models
section: 4.1 Deep-unfolded multivariate VMD for correlated multichannel signals
text:
4.1 Deep-unfolded multivariate VMD for correlated multichannel signals

TaskAlgorithm unrolling: a coupled multivariate optimisation algorithm rewritten as learnable layers, evaluated as decomposition and as a forecasting preprocessing module Recommended levelMSc (a narrower BSc variant is possible, see Bachelor scope) ComputeLight for the synthetic benchmark; moderate for the applied task (single 8+ GB consumer GPU) Starting paperAhmad, Wesemann, Waschkowski & Khalid, Adaptive Deep-Unfolded VMD, 2025


What you will do. Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) splits a signal into band-limited modes by solving a constrained optimisation problem with ADMM. A 2025 paper unrolls this ADMM iteration into a small stack of learnable layers (“UVMD”), replacing a fixed bandwidth hyperparameter with a learned one and cutting decomposition time roughly 250-fold — but only for a single channel at a time, applied independently channel by channel to multichannel data. Multivariate VMD (MVMD) already extends classical VMD to couple multiple channels through one shared, jointly estimated center frequency per mode. No deep-unfolded version of that coupled algorithm exists yet. You will design one.

Project goal. Unroll MVMD’s cross-channel frequency-coupling step into a learnable module that keeps the coupling genuine — rather than collapsing back into independent per-channel UVMD — and test whether coupling correlated channels, with the coupling weights themselves made learnable, improves decomposition accuracy, noise robustness and downstream task performance over both classical MVMD (accurate, slow) and independently-applied UVMD (fast, uncoupled).
Data. Required: a synthetic multichannel benchmark with known ground-truth modes, center frequencies and channel counts (2–32) at varied SNR, following the validation protocol in the VMD and MVMD papers — this is what the algorithm-design claims rest on. Required applied task: LargeST traffic forecasting (up to 8,600 California sensors, four regional subsets; also on Kaggle), the same benchmark the anchor paper uses — confirm its licence terms before allocation. Optional generalisation check: the CTU-UHB Intrapartum Cardiotocography Database (PhysioNet, open access, non-commercial use, 552 recordings), the same bivariate fetal heart rate / uterine contraction application MVMD’s own paper used.
Methods and starting code. Start from the anchor paper’s official UVMD implementation (uvmd.py) — both the baseline to beat (applied independently per channel) and the template to extend, since its unrolled ADMM layer is the single-channel building block. Use vmdpy as a numerically clean, non-unfolded reference for validating each unrolled layer. No Python port of classical MVMD exists yet; porting the official MATLAB implementation is an early, well-scoped first task and doubles as the classical baseline. For the applied task, reuse the anchor repository’s data pipeline and forecasting backbone so the decomposition module is the only substituted component.
Required baselines. Classical MVMD run to convergence; classical single-channel VMD applied independently per channel; UVMD (the anchor paper’s method) applied independently per channel — the direct competitor; the proposed jointly unrolled, learnably-weighted MVMD; and an ablation of the proposed method with the coupling step present but its channel weights fixed equal, to isolate whether coupling alone explains any gain or whether the learnable weighting does.
Evaluation. On the synthetic benchmark: per-mode reconstruction error against ground truth, center-frequency estimation error as a function of channel count and per-channel SNR, number of unrolled layers needed to match converged MVMD accuracy, and wall-clock decomposition time — reproduce the anchor paper’s speedup claim and check it survives adding coupling. On LargeST: MAE, RMSE and MAPE at prediction horizons 1–12 on at least two regions, plus decomposition time and trainable parameter count, comparing graph-neighbour channel groupings against all-channel pooling. Report at least three seeds for every learned method, and always report the fixed-weight ablation alongside any positive result.

Bachelor scope (if offered). Port classical MVMD to Python, unroll it with a fixed, non-learnable coupling step (skip the learnable channel-weighting question), and compare against per-channel UVMD and classical MVMD on the synthetic benchmark only — no applied dataset required. This is a reproduction-plus-one-extension study, smaller than the MSc contribution below.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Does a jointly unrolled, learnably-weighted multivariate VMD recover shared oscillatory structure across correlated channels more accurately and more robustly to per-channel noise than either classical MVMD or independently-applied single-channel UVMD — and does that advantage survive into a downstream forecasting task? The minimum contribution is (1) a correctly implemented coupled unrolled update, verified not to silently collapse into independent per-channel UVMD, (2) a learnable channel-weighting mechanism in the coupling step, motivated and ablated against equal-weight pooling, and (3) the full baseline comparison on both the synthetic benchmark and LargeST. Reproducing the anchor paper’s per-channel UVMD alone is a reproduction study, not the contribution.

Practical notes. Validate every unrolled layer against vmdpy’s classical fixed-point update before adding any learning. Write an early test that would fail if the implementation reduced to independent per-channel UVMDs (e.g. verify one channel’s output has a non-zero gradient with respect to another channel’s input) — the cross-channel coupling is the entire point of this project. Confirm LargeST’s licence before committing to it; the synthetic benchmark plus the openly licensed CTU-UHB database is a sufficient fallback applied study on its own. The anchor repository has no licence file — check with its authors before reusing its code beyond research and study.

title: Category 1 GNN applications for real-world data
text:
A graph is a way to represent entities and the relationships between them. The entities are called nodes and their relationships are called edges. Both may carry useful information: a customer node might contain age or location, a product node might contain category and price, and an edge might record that a customer bought or rated a product. Road sensors connected by roads, transactions linked by payments and atoms connected by chemical bonds are other examples.
A graph neural network (GNN) learns numerical representations, or embeddings, by combining a node’s own features with information from its neighbours. In the example, the model can use a customer’s previous purchases, the properties of products and patterns from nearby customers to score a new customer-product link. The same principle supports node classification (classify a transaction), link prediction (recommend a product), and graph-level prediction (predict a property of an entire molecule or sensor system).
The projects below begin with a practical decision: estimate remaining life, forecast traffic, detect illicit activity, recommend an item or screen a molecule. Students must define what the nodes and edges mean, choose the appropriate prediction level and test whether the graph adds value beyond a non-graph model.

title: Category 1 GNN applications for real-world data
section: 1.1 Remaining useful life prediction for aircraft engines
text:
1.1 Remaining useful life prediction for aircraft engines

TaskGraph-level temporal regression Recommended levelBSc or MSc ComputeVery light to light; CPU or 4 GB GPU Starting paperHuang, He and Sick, Spatio-Temporal Attention GNN for RUL, 2024


What you will do. Predict how many operating cycles remain before a turbofan engine fails. Each sensor channel becomes a node; edges express statistical or learned relationships among sensors. A temporal encoder then follows how the sensor graph changes as an engine ages.

Project goal. Given a recent window of readings from one engine, predict one remaining-life value. The scientific question is whether explicitly modelling sensor interactions improves over treating the measurements as an ordinary multivariate sequence.
Data. Use NASA C-MAPSS. Start with FD001: 100 training engines, 100 test engines, three operating-condition variables and 21 sensor channels. FD002–FD004 are optional transfer sets. Split by engine, never by windows from the same engine.
Methods and starting code. Linear or MLP regression, GRU/LSTM/TCN, GCN–GRU, GAT–GRU and the anchor spatiotemporal attention model. Compare correlation, random and learned sensor graphs. PHMGNNBenchmark and the GNN RUL benchmarking repository are useful code references; students should still document their own preprocessing.
Required baselines. A naive constant or degradation-stage baseline, one graph-free sequence model and one compact spatiotemporal GNN. The graph experiment must include a no-edge or random-edge control.
Evaluation. MAE or RMSE is primary; the asymmetric NASA score is optional. Report error by early, middle and late life. Fit normalization and graph construction on training engines only and report at least three seeds for MSc work.

Bachelor scope. Use FD001. Compare a GRU with one compact GNN, one graph construction and one random/no-edge ablation. Submit a documented pipeline and state whether the graph changes performance.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Can a sparse, time-varying sensor graph improve RUL accuracy and robustness when sensors become noisy or unavailable? Develop one graph-learning mechanism, compare it with fixed correlation and random graphs, and include missing-sensor, uncertainty or cross-subset transfer analysis. Merely rerunning an available implementation is not the contribution.

Practical notes. FD001 is easy to run. The main risks are window leakage, inconsistent RUL capping and comparing results produced with different normalization or scoring rules. Freeze these choices before modelling.

title: Category 1 GNN applications for real-world data
section: 1.2 Multi-horizon traffic forecasting with data-driven graph structure
text:
1.2 Multi-horizon traffic forecasting with data-driven graph structure

TaskNode-level temporal regression Recommended levelBSc or MSc ComputeLight to moderate; 4–8 GB GPU Starting paperLi et al., DCRNN, and Wu et al., Graph WaveNet


What you will do. Forecast traffic speed at every road sensor 15, 30 and 60 minutes ahead. The supplied road graph is a useful starting point, but congestion can couple sensors in ways that do not follow the shortest road distance.

Project goal. Determine whether a road-distance graph, a training-only correlation graph or a learned graph gives the most reliable forecasts, especially at the 60-minute horizon.
Data. Use METR-LA from the official DCRNN repository: 207 sensors and 34,272 five-minute observations. PEMS-BAY with 325 sensors is the optional transfer target. Use the established chronological 70/10/20 split.
Methods and starting code. Historical average, linear regression, GRU, DCRNN, STGCN, Graph WaveNet code, MTGNN and a compact Transformer. A dynamic graph should be sparse or low-rank so its cost is explicit.
Required baselines. Historical average, graph-free GRU/Transformer and one fixed-graph spatiotemporal GNN. Compare supplied distance adjacency, training-only correlation adjacency, a single learned static adjacency and the proposed variant.
Evaluation. MAE is primary; report RMSE and MAPE at 15/30/60 minutes. Fit scalers and correlation graphs on the training period only. For dynamic adjacency, report memory, latency and edge stability as well as forecast error.

Bachelor scope. Compare historical average, GRU and one spatiotemporal GNN on the supplied graph. Add one no-edge or randomized-edge control.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Does a time-of-day and traffic-regime-conditioned sparse adjacency improve long-horizon forecasting over both the road graph and a single learned static graph? Match depth and width, use at least three seeds, and examine whether rush-hour edges differ from free-flow edges and whether learned edges correspond to plausible topology. A robustness-and-transfer route using missing sensors and METR-LA to PEMS-BAY transfer is an alternative, but it must be narrowed to one preregistered question.

Practical notes. Per-timestep dense adjacency is unnecessarily expensive and unstable. Profile early and enforce top-k sparsity or low rank. This project and Project 3.1 both use traffic data, but this one studies the graph itself; Project 3.1 studies unseen-sensor representations.

title: Category 1 GNN applications for real-world data
text:
1.3 Illicit Bitcoin transaction detection

TaskNode classification on a temporal graph Recommended levelBSc or MSc ComputeModerate; sparse mini-batches on 4–8 GB GPU Starting paperWeber et al., Anti-Money Laundering in Bitcoin


What you will do. Each Bitcoin transaction is a node, and directed payment flows are edges. The model predicts whether a labelled transaction is licit or illicit while respecting the order in which transactions occurred.

Project goal. Test whether neighbourhood information helps detect rare illicit transactions beyond the transaction’s own features, without allowing information from future time steps to leak into training.
Data. Use the PyG Elliptic Bitcoin Temporal loader: 203,769 transaction nodes, 234,355 edges, 165 features and 49 time steps. Unknown labels are unlabelled, not negatives.
Methods and starting code. Logistic regression or gradient boosting on node features; GCN, GraphSAGE or GAT; EvolveGCN or TGN for an MSc extension. Use class weighting or focal loss only after establishing an unweighted baseline. PyG’s loader is the recommended data starting point.
Required baselines. Feature-only classifier, static GCN/GraphSAGE and a no-edge or random-edge control. A temporal model is required only for the MSc temporal route.
Evaluation. Chronological splits only. Use AUPRC or illicit-class F1 as the primary metric and report illicit recall at a fixed false-positive rate. Exclude unknown nodes from supervised loss and labelled-node metrics; examine performance over time.

Bachelor scope. Compare a feature-only model with GCN or GraphSAGE and analyse how edge removal changes performance. Include class-imbalance and per-time-step error analysis.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Can a temporally calibrated GNN remain useful under concept drift and missing transaction edges? Add one temporal mechanism or uncertainty method, test edge deletion and temporal shift, and connect threshold choices to investigator workload. A negative result may show that features dominate topology during particular regimes.

Practical notes. Random splitting makes this task unrealistically easy. Keep time ordering, labels and threshold selection fixed across methods. Mini-batching or snapshot processing keeps the graph manageable.

title: Category 1 GNN applications for real-world data
section: 1.4 Graph-based movie recommendation with accuracy and coverage
text:
1.4 Graph-based movie recommendation with accuracy and coverage

TaskLink prediction and ranking on a bipartite graph Recommended levelBSc recommended; limited MSc scope ComputeVery light; CPU or low-memory GPU Starting paperHe et al., LightGCN, SIGIR 2020


What you will do. Represent users and movies as two node types. A rating or interaction is an edge. The model scores unseen user–movie pairs and recommends a ranked list, while also checking whether recommendations collapse onto popular titles.

Project goal. Measure whether message passing improves top-k ranking over popularity and matrix factorization and whether any gain comes at the cost of catalogue coverage.
Data. Use MovieLens 100K: 100,000 timestamped ratings from about 1,000 users on 1,700 movies, roughly a 5 MB download.
Methods and starting code. Popularity, item/user nearest neighbours, matrix factorization and LightGCN. The official LightGCN repository is a reference, but its data protocol must be adapted transparently to MovieLens 100K.
Required baselines. Popularity and matrix factorization are mandatory; LightGCN is the graph model. Use identical candidate sets and negative-sampling rules.
Evaluation. Use a per-user chronological split and remove validation/test interactions from the training graph. NDCG@20 or Recall@20 is primary; also report catalogue coverage and average popularity of recommended items.

Bachelor scope. Compare popularity, matrix factorization and LightGCN. Study depth or negative sampling and report both accuracy and coverage.


Master research question and contribution. For an MSc project, use a narrower research question such as: Can a calibrated diversity objective improve long-tail exposure without materially reducing NDCG? This requires user-activity and item-popularity subgroup analysis, multiple seeds and a defined Pareto trade-off. Without this extension, the project is suitable for Bachelor scope.

Practical notes. The dataset and baseline setup are small. The principal pitfalls are leakage from future interactions and evaluation on sampled negatives that differ across methods.

title: Category 1 GNN applications for real-world data
section: 1.5 Molecular HIV activity prediction with calibrated GNNs
text:
1.5 Molecular HIV activity prediction with calibrated GNNs

TaskGraph classification Recommended levelBSc or MSc ComputeLight to moderate; 4–8 GB GPU Starting paperHu et al., Open Graph Benchmark


What you will do. A molecule is a graph: atoms are nodes and bonds are edges. Predict whether the complete molecule is active in the HIV benchmark assay and test whether confidence estimates remain useful on molecular scaffolds not seen during training.

Project goal. Compare learned graph representations with established chemical fingerprints under the official out-of-scaffold split.
Data. Use OGB ogbg-molhiv: 41,127 molecular graphs, official scaffold split and official ROC-AUC evaluator. The OGB loader guide handles download and split indices.
Methods and starting code. Morgan fingerprints with logistic regression or random forest; GCN; GIN/GINE; PNA; compact GraphGPS. OGB provides baseline code, and PyG provides the layers and loader.
Required baselines. Fingerprint classifier, GCN and GIN/GINE. Bond-feature and pooling ablations are required. If self-supervised pretraining is added, follow the shared SSL protocol.
Evaluation. Use only the official scaffold split and evaluator. ROC-AUC is primary; AUPRC, Brier score or expected calibration error are supporting metrics. Report at least three seeds. Do not compare scaffold-split results with random-split figures.

Bachelor scope. Compare fingerprints, GCN and GIN/GINE and inspect errors on unfamiliar scaffolds. Include one bond-feature or pooling ablation.


Master research question and contribution. Research question: Can uncertainty-aware training improve calibration on held-out scaffolds without sacrificing discrimination? Compare temperature scaling, deep ensembles or a compact evidential/uncertainty variant on identical predictions and report both performance and calibration by scaffold novelty. A self-supervised route is possible, but it must be distinct from Project 3.3.

Practical notes. The dataset is well established and manageable. The main danger is silently changing the split or selecting a threshold on test data.

title: Selection guidance
text:
A simple decision process

Choose the task, not the fashionable model: node classification, link prediction, graph prediction, temporal forecasting or representation learning.
Download the data and run one complete baseline on a small subset before the formal project begins.
Write a one-sentence research question and identify the comparison that could falsify the proposed explanation.
Freeze the split, primary metric and compute budget before extensive development.
Treat the authors’ repository as an executable specification—not as the thesis contribution.

title: Selection guidance
text:
Week-one feasibility checklist

Obtain access to the exact dataset and record its version, size, licence or data agreement, and release date or extraction period.
Run the simplest baseline from raw input to final metric on a small subset.
Identify the independent split unit and verify that it cannot cross train and test.
Record the anchor paper, repository version and preprocessing deviations.
Estimate training time and peak memory before planning seeds or ablations.
For MSc work, write the question, proposed mechanism, main alternative explanation and minimum viable ablation table.

title: Selection guidance
text:
Recurring failure modes

Comparing with a number produced by a different split, metric, horizon, shot count or evaluation level.
Using windows from the same physical unit in both training and test sets.
Calling an authors’ repository run a research contribution.
Reporting only in-distribution performance when transfer or cold start is the motivation.
Omitting the random frozen encoder in a self-supervised study.
Treating a recent preprint figure as a settled benchmark.
Expanding to a second dataset before the first pipeline and evaluation protocol are stable.

Select one primary question, fix the evaluation protocol before extensive experimentation and report negative as well as positive results.
The Tetra Pak project is included as Project 2.1. A Siemens Gamesa project may be offered separately when its scope and data access are confirmed.
